lead: Two liquid phases in a beaker, or a crystal sitting in its own solution, are both phase-equilibrium problems. The rule is the same as for vapour-liquid: every component has equal fugacity in every phase present. Liquid-liquid equality gives the tie lines of solvent extraction. Solid-liquid equality gives the solubility curve and the eutectic. Industry uses these equations for extracting essential oils, crystallising sugar and salt, and predicting wax deposition in pipelines.
prereq: You need: 6.1, 6.4, and Unit 5 for activity coefficients and excess Gibbs energy.

blocks.text: Put a pure solid 1 in a liquid and stir. The solid dissolves until the liquid solution is saturated. At equilibrium the fugacity of the solid equals the fugacity of component 1 in the liquid. For a pure solid, the fugacity ratio to its pure liquid at the same T and P follows from the fusion process. With ΔC<sub>p</sub> ≈ 0, the result is:

blocks.where: x₁ is the mole fraction of the solid in the saturated liquid; γ₁ is its activity coefficient in that liquid; Δh<sub>fus</sub> is the enthalpy of fusion of the pure solid in J/mol; R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹; T is the temperature in K; T<sub>m</sub> is the normal melting point of the pure solid in K.

blocks.text: Set γ₁ = 1 to get the ideal solubility. For a non-ideal solution with γ₁ > 1, this ideal value is too high; the real solubility is lower. A larger Δh<sub>fus</sub> gives a steeper curve and lower solubility at the same T, as the figure shows. This equation is the working tool for crystallisation design: choose T to reach a required x₁.

sections.h3: Liquid-liquid equilibrium: tie lines and extraction

blocks.text: Two liquid phases α and β form when two components dislike each other enough. At equilibrium, every component i has equal fugacity in both phases. Using the same pure-liquid standard state in both phases gives:

blocks.where: x<sub>i</sub><sup>α</sup> and x<sub>i</sub><sup>β</sup> are mole fractions of component i in phases α and β; γ<sub>i</sub><sup>α</sup> and γ<sub>i</sub><sup>β</sup> are the corresponding activity coefficients.

blocks.text: A tie line joins two liquid compositions that coexist. The binodal curve is the boundary of the two-phase region. In a ternary diagram the tie lines shrink to a point called the plait point. Only the ratio of activity coefficients comes out of one tie line: γ<sub>i</sub><sup>α</sup>/γ<sub>i</sub><sup>β</sup> = x<sub>i</sub><sup>β</sup>/x<sub>i</sub><sup>α</sup>. To get individual γ values, use an activity-coefficient model plus the Gibbs-Duhem equation from Unit 5.

Solvent extraction uses this. The distribution coefficient is K<sub>D</sub> = x<sub>i</sub><sup>β</sup>/x<sub>i</sub><sup>α</sup>. A large K<sub>D</sub> means the solute prefers the solvent phase β. Choose a solvent with high K<sub>D</sub> and low mutual solubility with the feed phase. The same equations describe extraction of essential oils and recovery of acetic acid from water.

sections.h3: Three phases, eutectics and industrial uses

blocks.text: When two liquid phases and a vapour are present, every component has equal fugacity in all three phases: f<sub>i</sub><sup>L1</sup> = f<sub>i</sub><sup>L2</sup> = f<sub>i</sub><sup>V</sup>. For a binary at three phases, F = C − P + 2 = 2 − 3 + 2 = 1. Fix T and the three-phase pressure is a single number. This is the heteroazeotrope used to dry solvents by distillation.

Two pure solids in a liquid give a eutectic. At the eutectic temperature the liquid has a fixed composition and both solids crystallise together. Cool a solution below its saturation temperature and one solid appears; cool below the eutectic and both appear.

Crystallisation uses cooling or evaporation to make x₁ exceed the solubility. Sugar and salt are made this way. In pipelines, wax dissolves in warm crude oil and crystallises when the oil cools; the SLE equation predicts the wax appearance temperature, and inhibitors stop the deposit. In all these calculations, keep γ and the correct standard state.

figure.caption: At the melting point both curves meet at x₁ = 1; below it the solid with the larger heat of fusion has the lower ideal solubility. The worked example reads the upper curve at 300 K.

spec.title: Ideal solubility falling as the heat of fusion rises
spec.aria: Ideal solubility against temperature for two solids melting at 330 K; both curves meet at the melting point x₁ = 1, and the solid with the larger heat of fusion dissolves far less at any lower temperature.

examples.question: A solid melts at 330 K with Δh<sub>fus</sub> = 20.0 kJ/mol. (a) Find its ideal solubility as a mole fraction in a liquid at 300 K. (b) Find the real solubility if the activity coefficient of the solid in the liquid is γ₁ = 1.8.
steps: Convert the heat of fusion: Δh<sub>fus</sub> = 20.0 kJ/mol = 20000 J/mol. Use R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.
For the ideal solubility set γ₁ = 1: ln x₁ = −0.72896, so x₁ = exp(−0.72896) = 0.4824.
For the real solubility use ln(x₁γ₁) = −0.72896. Then x₁γ₁ = 0.4824, so x₁ = 0.4824/1.8 = 0.268.
examples.answer: (a) The ideal solubility is x₁ = 0.4824. (b) With γ₁ = 1.8 the real solubility is x₁ = 0.268.
examples.check:
import math
R = 8.314
dh = 20000.0
Tm = 330.0
T = 300.0
gamma = 1.8
ln_x_gamma = -dh/R*(1/T - 1/Tm)
x_ideal = math.exp(ln_x_gamma)
x_real = x_ideal/gamma
print(round(x_ideal, 4))
print(round(x_real, 4))

traps: Dropping γ₁ in a solid-liquid calculation when γ₁ > 1 and then believing the high ideal solubility obtained.
Using different standard states for the two liquid phases in an LLE calculation; then the activity coefficients cannot be compared.
Putting Δh<sub>fus</sub> in kJ/mol while R is in J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, or putting T in °C instead of K.
For a binary at three phases, treating F as 2. At fixed T the three-phase pressure is one value, not a range.
Confusing the binodal curve (phase boundary) with a tie line (two coexisting compositions).

quiz.q: State the fugacity equality for liquid-liquid equilibrium of component i in phases α and β.
quiz.a: f<sub>i</sub><sup>α</sup> = f<sub>i</sub><sup>β</sup>, which with the same pure-liquid standard state gives x<sub>i</sub><sup>α</sup>γ<sub>i</sub><sup>α</sup> = x<sub>i</sub><sup>β</sup>γ<sub>i</sub><sup>β</sup>.

quiz.q: Why does one tie line give only the ratio γ<sub>i</sub><sup>α</sup>/γ<sub>i</sub><sup>β</sup> and not each activity coefficient separately?
quiz.a: The equality x<sub>i</sub><sup>α</sup>γ<sub>i</sub><sup>α</sup> = x<sub>i</sub><sup>β</sup>γ<sub>i</sub><sup>β</sup> contains one equation per component. Rearranged, it fixes the ratio γ<sub>i</sub><sup>α</sup>/γ<sub>i</sub><sup>β</sup> = x<sub>i</sub><sup>β</sup>/x<sub>i</sub><sup>α</sup>. Splitting the ratio needs a model plus Gibbs-Duhem.

quiz.q: A solid has Δh<sub>fus</sub> = 30.0 kJ/mol and T<sub>m</sub> = 330 K. Find its ideal solubility in a liquid at 300 K.
For a solid in a liquid with γ₁ = 1.8 at 300 K, explain why the real solubility is lower than the ideal solubility and by what factor.
quiz.a: The equation is ln(x₁γ₁) = constant. For fixed T, x₁γ₁ is fixed at the ideal value. If γ₁ > 1, x₁ must be smaller. Here x₁,real = x₁,ideal/γ₁ = 0.4824/1.8 = 0.268, a factor of 1.8 lower.

quiz.q: In an extraction, the solute mole fraction is 0.05 in the feed phase α and 0.35 in the solvent phase β. Find K<sub>D</sub> = x<sub>i</sub><sup>β</sup>/x<sub>i</sub><sup>α</sup>.
What is a eutectic in a two-solid system?
quiz.a: A eutectic is the liquid composition and temperature at which two pure solids coexist with one liquid. At that point both solids crystallise together and the liquid composition is fixed.

quiz.q: For a binary system with two liquid phases and one vapour phase, why is the three-phase pressure a single value at a fixed temperature?
quiz.a: Three phases give P = 3 and C = 2, so F = C − P + 2 = 1. The only free intensive variable is one; fixing T fixes the three-phase pressure. The equalities f<sub>i</sub><sup>L1</sup> = f<sub>i</sub><sup>L2</sup> = f<sub>i</sub><sup>V</sup> for both components supply the equations that set it.

beyond: Not for the exam. Solvent selection for extraction now uses computer-aided molecular design with activity-coefficient models. Solid-liquid equilibria matter in battery electrolytes, pharmaceutical cocrystals and gas hydrates. Search for solid-liquid equilibrium activity coefficient, ternary LLE plait point, and wax appearance temperature.
